title: Morning (II.10)
hookLine: before the phone lights up, Francis de Sales asks for a few minutes: thank, look ahead, and hand the day over
tomorrow: the day went badly. why does Francis start the night with thanks?

lines: FIVE-FORTY, AND THE PHONE IS GLOWING.
HAND IT OVER BEFORE YOU LIVE IT.
cards: Five-forty. The alarm is off, the room is still dark, and the phone on the nightstand is already glowing: a group chat, an email, a reminder about something due. One swipe and the day has started without you.

Francis de Sales, a bishop who wrote the Introduction to the Devout Life for people with jobs and households, asks for a few minutes before any of that. Not the long meditation; that has its own hour.
A short exercise for every morning, the rushed ones too. And it ends with a strange move: you hand the day over before you've lived a minute of it.

teach.b: It comes in four steps. First, adore and thank. Begin, Francis says, by adoring God and thanking him for keeping you through the night, and if anything in the night went wrong, ask pardon.
Second, remember what the day is for. This day, he says, is given you so that you can gain the day of eternity, so make a firm resolve to use it well.

Third, look ahead. Think through what the day will probably hold: the work, the people, the chances to serve God, and the temptations that could come with them, to anger, to vanity, to some other slip. Then get ready.
If you know you'll deal with someone quick to anger, settle now on gentle words. Fourth, the heart in your hands. Humble yourself, he says, knowing you can't carry out these good plans alone.

Then take your heart in your hands, as it were, and offer it to God with everything you've resolved, asking him to keep it and strengthen it. He adds that all of it can be done briefly, before you leave your room.
Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the planning sits third, between the thanks and the offering. It isn't a to-do list.
It's a plan made in company.

how: Some Catholic prayer books include a short morning offering, said on waking, that gives the day's prayers, works and sufferings to God; some people add a quick look at the day ahead.

o: a fast kept until noon each day
a short exercise to begin the day with God
the first hour of prayer before work

games.q: the morning, in order — tap the pairs.
p: for being kept through the night
the day is given to gain eternity
the work, the people, the temptations
the heart in your hands, given to God

s: Francis's morning exercise is mostly about getting more done
the planning sits between thanks and offering. it's a plan made in company, not a productivity trick.
he says the whole exercise can be done briefly, before you leave your room
a few minutes, not another hour.
he tells you to prepare for the temptations the day might bring
anger, vanity, other slips: see them coming and settle how you'll meet them.

games.q: you know a family dinner tonight will put you across from the uncle who always starts an argument. it's morning. what does Francis's third step look like?
o: decide now on one calm answer for when he starts.
skip dinner so the temptation never comes.
hope it goes fine and deal with it when it happens.
games.why: Francis says to foresee the day's meetings and their temptations and prepare the means: if someone is quick to anger, settle on gentle words ahead of time.

practice: Pick one moment in the next day that could go sideways: a meeting, a practice, a hard conversation. Through the sit, decide one way you'll meet it, the way Francis settles on gentle words before seeing someone short-tempered.
If you pray, you can end by offering the day, heart in hand.

wordCard.voice: Morning. In Francis's book, a short exercise to begin the day: thanks, purpose, a look ahead, and an offering.

carryVoice: Your line: plan the day with god. The plan comes after the thanks and before the offering. Until tomorrow.
